subject: math
title: Graphs and Functions: Slope, Intercepts, Equations of Lines, and Function Notation
objectives: You will read and plot points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
You will find slope from two points, a graph, a table, or an equation, and explain slope as a rate of change.
You will find intercepts and write equations of lines in slope-intercept, point-slope, and standard form, including parallel and perpendicular lines.
You will use function notation and decide whether a relation is a function.
You will interpret graphs of real-world situations and compare functions given as equations, tables, and graphs.

slides.title: Week 9 Math: Graphs and Functions
slides.board:
Graphs and Functions

Slope, Intercepts, Equations of Lines, and Function Notation

  • Read and plot points in all four quadrants
  • Find slope from two points, a graph, a table, or an equation
  • Find intercepts and write equations of lines, including parallel and perpendicular lines
  • Use function notation and test whether a relation is a function
  • Read real-world graphs and compare functions

Today: warm-up, the coordinate plane, slope, equations of lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, functions, graphs, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 9. Last week you solved equations; this week you see what an equation looks like as a picture. A line on a graph is just every solution of an equation like y = 2x + 1 drawn as dots that run together. A handful of ideas, slope and the y-intercept above all, unlock most of the graphing questions on the GED. Keep graph paper and two colored pens nearby, because today we sketch everything.
ask: When you see a graph in the news or on a bill, what is the first thing you look at? (expected answer: any; steer toward the title and the labels on the axes)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); coordinate plane 4 min (slides 3–4); slope 12 min (slides 5–11); equations of lines 10 min (slides 12–15); parallel and perpendicular 7 min (slides 16–18); functions 7 min (slides 19–21); graphs and comparing 7 min (slides 22–23); you-do, GED question, strategy and recap 8 min (slides 24–28). If you fall behind, assign slide 25 as homework.

slides.title: Warm-up: Last Week's Equations
slides.board:
Review from Week 8. Work on paper.

  1. Solve 3x − 7 = 11.
  2. Solve 4(x + 2) = 2x + 14.
  3. Solve −2x + 5 ≥ 13.
  4. Solve the system y = 2x and x + y = 12.
  5. Solve 3y = 6x − 12 for y.
steps: 3. Subtract 5: −2x ≥ 8. Divide by −2 and flip the sign: x ≤ −4.
4. Substitute: x + 2x = 12, so 3x = 12 and x = 4; y = 2(4) = 8. Solution (4, 8).

notes.say: These five problems are all from last week, and three of them lead straight into today. Problem 4 has an answer that is a point, (4, 8): that is where two lines cross on a graph. Problem 5 turns an equation into the form y = mx + b, which is the most useful form of a line today. Take about three minutes and then read me your answers.
ask: What did you get for number 3, and why did the sign change? (expected answer: x ≤ −4; dividing by a negative reverses the inequality)
In number 5, did you divide every term by 3? (expected answer: yes; 6x ÷ 3 = 2x and −12 ÷ 3 = −4)
notes.watch: On number 3, x ≥ −4 means the student forgot to flip the sign. On number 5, y = 6x − 4 or y = 2x − 12 means only one term was divided by 3; that same slip shows up today when we change 2x + 3y = 12 into y = mx + b, so name it now.

slides.title: The Coordinate Plane
slides.board:
• The x-axis runs left and right; the y-axis runs up and down. They cross at the origin, (0, 0).
  • An ordered pair (x, y): move across first, then up or down.
QuadrantSignsPoint
I (upper right)(+, +)P(3, 4)
II (upper left)(−, +)Q(−3, 4)
III (lower left)(−, −)R(−3, −4)
IV (lower right)(+, −)S(3, −4)

notes.say: Think of the coordinate plane as a map with an address for every spot. The address has two parts, and the order matters: the first number is how far you walk across, and the second is how far you climb up or go down. The quadrants are numbered I to IV going counterclockwise, starting at the upper right. A point sitting on an axis, like (0, 4), is not in any quadrant.
ask: What are the signs of a point in Quadrant II? (expected answer: x negative, y positive)
Where is (0, −5)? (expected answer: on the y-axis, 5 below the origin; not in a quadrant)
notes.watch: The most common slip is swapping the coordinates: plotting (3, −2) as 3 down and 2 right. Have the student say “across, then up or down” out loud for the first few points.

slides.title: Read Points on the Plane
slides.board:
Name the coordinates of each point and the quadrant it is in.

Method: start at the origin. Count across to the point first (x), then up or down (y).
steps: D: no move across, 4 up → (0, 4). It is on the y-axis, so it is not in any quadrant.

notes.say: I will do the first one out loud. Start at the origin, walk across to point A: that is 4 to the right, so x is positive 4. Now go down to A: 2 down, so y is negative 2. A is (4, −2) and it is in the lower right, Quadrant IV. Your turn to tell me B before I reveal it.
ask: What are the coordinates of B? (expected answer: (−5, 3))
Why is D not in a quadrant? (expected answer: it is on the y-axis; its x-coordinate is 0)
notes.watch: If the student names C as (−5, −2), they counted up or down first. Point back to the rule: across first.

slides.title: Slope: Rise Over Run
slides.board:
Slope m measures how steep a line is and which way it goes.

m = rise / run = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1)

LineSlope
Rises left to rightPositive
Falls left to rightNegative
Horizontal (y = 4)Zero
Vertical (x = −4)Undefined

notes.say: Slope answers one question: when I move one step to the right, how far does the line go up or down? Read every line from left to right, the way you read a sentence. If the line climbs, the slope is positive; if it falls, the slope is negative. A flat line has zero rise, so its slope is 0. A vertical line, like the dark line x = −4 on the graph, has zero run, and since we cannot divide by zero, its slope is undefined. The slope formula is on the GED formula sheet, so you do not have to memorize it, but you do have to use it correctly.
ask: Which line on the graph has a negative slope? (expected answer: y = −x − 2; it falls from left to right)
What is the slope of the line y = 4? (expected answer: 0)
notes.watch: Students often mix up zero and undefined. Anchor it: a horizontal road is flat, so you can walk it (slope 0); a vertical wall cannot be walked at all (undefined).

slides.title: Slope from Two Points
slides.board:
Find the slope of the line through (−1, 6) and (3, −2).

m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1)
steps: Check by switching the order: (6 − (−2)) / (−1 − 3) = 8 / (−4) = −2. Same answer. The line falls, so a negative slope makes sense.

notes.say: Label the points first; it takes five seconds and prevents most mistakes. Then y on top, x on the bottom, and subtract in the same order in both places. Either point can be point 1, as long as you stay consistent. Last, look at the graph: the line falls from left to right, so a negative answer is a good sign.
ask: What is 3 − (−1)? (expected answer: 4)
Does the sign of the answer match the picture? (expected answer: yes; the line falls, so the slope is negative)
notes.watch: Watch for 3 − (−1) written as 2, which gives a slope of −4. Have the student rewrite “minus a negative” as “plus” before computing.

slides.title: Slope from a Graph
slides.board:
Find the slope of the line shown.

Method: pick two points where the line crosses grid corners exactly. Count the rise (up +, down −), then the run to the right.
steps: The line crosses grid corners at (0, 1) and (3, 3).
Run: from x = 0 to x = 3 is 3 to the right.
Rise: from y = 1 to y = 3 is 2 up.
Check with another pair, (−3, −1) and (0, 1): up 2, right 3 again. A line has the same slope everywhere.

notes.say: The dark slope triangle on the graph shows the run and the rise. I like to count the run first, always moving to the right, and then ask how far up or down I had to go to get back to the line. Pick points where the line passes exactly through a grid corner; guessing at a point between grid lines gives a wrong slope. The slope of a line is the same no matter which two points you pick.
ask: Is the slope positive or negative, just by looking? (expected answer: positive; the line rises)
What would you get if you put the run on top? (expected answer: 3/2, which is wrong)
notes.watch: Students who answer 3/2 have run over rise. A memory hook: you climb the ladder (rise) before you walk (run), so rise goes on top.

slides.title: Slope Four Ways, Together
slides.board:
Find each slope. Say the change in y and the change in x before you divide.

  1. Through (−5, 2) and (1, −1)
  2. Through (2, 7) and (2, −3)
  3. From the table:
    x04812
    y5111723
  4. Through (−4, 3) and (5, 3)
steps: 2. (−3 − 7) / (2 − 2) = −10 / 0. You cannot divide by 0: the slope is undefined. The line is vertical, x = 2.
3. y goes up 6 each time x goes up 4: 6 / 4 = 3/2

notes.say: Let's work these together. For each one, tell me the change in y and the change in x first, then the slope. Two of these are special cases on purpose: watch what happens when the x-values match or the y-values match.
ask: In number 2, what is the change in x? (expected answer: 0, so the slope is undefined)
In number 3, why is the slope not 6? (expected answer: x goes up by 4, not by 1, so divide 6 by 4)
notes.watch: On number 2, a student who writes 0 has switched the two special cases; 0 on the bottom means undefined, 0 on the top means slope 0. On number 3, the answer 6 means they forgot to divide by the change in x.

slides.title: Slope as a Rate of Change
slides.board:
In a real-world graph or table, slope is a rate:

slope = change in output / change in input   (units: output units per input unit)

SituationSlope means
Cost vs. hoursdollars per hour
Distance vs. timemiles per hour (speed)
Water left vs. minutesgallons per minute (negative if draining)

Key words: per, each, every, rate.

notes.say: On the GED, most slope questions come dressed in real life. The slope is how fast one thing changes compared with another, and its units are always “output units per input unit.” If the quantity is going down, like water draining from a tank, the rate is negative. In a table, find the change between two rows in both columns and divide; if the input jumps by 2 or 5 each row, you must divide by that jump.
ask: A plumber charges $65 per hour plus a $40 trip fee. Which number is the slope? (expected answer: 65 dollars per hour)
A pool loses 30 gallons every 10 minutes. What is the rate of change? (expected answer: −3 gallons per minute)
notes.watch: Students often treat the starting fee as the rate because it appears first in the problem. Ask: “Which number gets multiplied by the hours?”

slides.title: Rate and Starting Value from a Table
slides.board:
A moving company's charges are shown. Write an equation for the cost C after h hours, then find the cost of a 7.5-hour move.

Hours (h)0246
Cost C ($)3070110150
steps: Starting value: at h = 0 the cost is $30 (a flat fee).

notes.say: Every linear situation has two numbers: a rate and a starting value. The rate is the slope, and the starting value is the output when the input is 0, which is the y-intercept. Here the table hands us h = 0 directly, so the starting value is $30. Notice that the cost goes up by 40 between rows, but the hours go up by 2, so the rate is 20, not 40.
ask: What does the 30 mean in this situation? (expected answer: a $30 flat fee charged even for 0 hours)
What would the cost be for 3 hours? (expected answer: 20(3) + 30 = $90)
notes.watch: The answer C = 40h + 30 means the student did not divide by the 2-hour jump. Test it: 40(2) + 30 = 110, not 70, so it fails the table.

slides.title: Your Turn: Slope
slides.board:
Three minutes. Work on paper, then tell me your answers.

  1. Find the slope through (4, 9) and (−2, 6).
  2. Find the slope through (0, −3) and (4, 5).
  3. A tank holds 80 gallons at 0 minutes, 65 gallons at 5 minutes, and 50 gallons at 10 minutes. What is the rate of change?
  4. Is the slope through (−1, 4) and (−1, −2) zero or undefined?

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting the clock for three minutes. Label your points before you subtract, and check the sign of each answer against what the situation is doing. When time is up, read me your four answers.
ask: Read me your answers. (expected answer: 1/2, 2, −3 gallons per minute, undefined)
notes.answer: (1) (6 − 9) / (−2 − 4) = −3 / −6 = 1/2   (2) (5 − (−3)) / (4 − 0) = 8 / 4 = 2   (3) (65 − 80) / (5 − 0) = −15 / 5 = −3 gallons per minute   (4) the x-values are equal, so the run is 0 and the slope is undefined (vertical line x = −1)
notes.watch: An answer of −1/2 on number 1 comes from subtracting in a different order on top and bottom. An answer of 3 or −15 on number 3 means the student dropped the sign or forgot to divide by the 5-minute jump.

slides.title: Intercepts and y = mx + b
slides.board:
• y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis. Set x = 0. Point (0, b).
  • x-intercept: where the line crosses the x-axis. Set y = 0. Point (a, 0).

Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b   (m = slope, b = y-intercept)

y = 2x − 4: slope 2, y-intercept (0, −4). Set y = 0: 2x = 4, so x-intercept (2, 0).

notes.say: An intercept is where the line crosses an axis. Anywhere on the y-axis, x is 0, so to find the y-intercept you plug in x = 0. Anywhere on the x-axis, y is 0, so to find the x-intercept you plug in y = 0. When an equation is in the form y = mx + b, you can read the slope and the y-intercept straight off it. To graph it, plot the y-intercept, then use the slope to step to a second point: from (0, −4), go up 2 and right 1.
ask: In y = −3x + 7, what are the slope and the y-intercept? (expected answer: slope −3, y-intercept (0, 7))
In a word problem, what does b usually stand for? (expected answer: the starting value, such as a fee or a starting balance)
notes.watch: Students mix up which variable to set to 0. Say it as a rule: “To find where you cross the x-axis, kill the y.”

slides.title: Standard Form: Intercepts and Slope
slides.board:
For the line 2x + 3y = 12, find both intercepts and the slope.

Method: set y = 0, then x = 0. For the slope, solve for y.
steps: x-intercept: set y = 0. 2x = 12, so x = 6. Point (6, 0).
y-intercept: set x = 0. 3y = 12, so y = 4. Point (0, 4).
Slope: solve for y. 3y = −2x + 12. Divide every term by 3: y = −(2/3)x + 4. Slope −2/3.

notes.say: An equation like 2x + 3y = 12 is in standard form. The intercepts are quick: cover up one variable by setting it to 0, and solve. For the slope, solve the equation for y, and divide every single term by the number in front of y. Then check: the two intercepts are two points on the line, so they give the same slope.
ask: Why is the slope negative? (expected answer: the line falls; or, moving 2x to the other side makes it −2x)
notes.watch: The most common error is y = −2x + 4: the student divided the 12 by 3 but not the −2x. Remind them that every term gets divided.

slides.title: Equation of a Line Through Two Points
slides.board:
Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through (−4, −1) and (4, 5).

Point-slope form: y − y1 = m(x − x1)
steps: Check with the other point: (3/4)(−4) + 2 = −3 + 2 = −1. Correct.

notes.say: Two points are all you need for a line. Step one is always the slope. Step two, put the slope and either point into point-slope form, which is on the formula sheet, and simplify to y = mx + b. Another way that works just as well: put the slope and one point into y = mx + b and solve for b. Always finish by testing the point you did not use.
ask: What is 4 − (−4)? (expected answer: 8)
Solve it the other way: 5 = (3/4)(4) + b. What is b? (expected answer: 5 = 3 + b, so b = 2)
notes.watch: With a point like (−4, −1), students often write y − 1 = m(x − 4). Point-slope subtracts the coordinates, so it becomes y + 1 = m(x + 4).

slides.title: Writing Equations Together
slides.board:
1. Slope −2, through (3, 1)
  2. Through (−2, 1) and (2, 9)
  3. The line on the graph
  4. Find both intercepts of 5x − 2y = 10.

Write 1–3 in y = mx + b form.
steps: 3. y-intercept (0, 3). From (0, 3) to (2, 2): down 1, right 2, so m = −1/2: y = −(1/2)x + 3.

notes.say: Let's build these equations together. For each one, tell me the slope first and then the y-intercept. On number 3, read the y-intercept off the graph, then count the slope between two marked points.
ask: In number 3, is the slope positive or negative? (expected answer: negative; the line falls)
In number 4, what is −2y = 10 solved for y? (expected answer: y = −5)
notes.watch: On number 3, the answer y = −2x + 3 means run over rise. On number 4, the answer (0, 5) means the student lost the negative when dividing by −2.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
slides.board:
• Parallel lines never meet: same slope, different y-intercepts.
  • Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle: slopes are opposite reciprocals (flip the fraction and change the sign). The slopes multiply to −1.
SlopeParallelPerpendicular
22−1/2
−3/4−3/44/3
0 (horizontal)0undefined (vertical)

notes.say: Parallel lines are like railroad tracks: they rise at exactly the same rate, so they have the same slope, and they never meet. Perpendicular lines cross to make a perfect corner. Their slopes are opposite reciprocals: flip the fraction upside down and change the sign. You need both moves. A quick test: multiply the two slopes, and if you get −1, they are perpendicular.
ask: What slope is perpendicular to 5? (expected answer: −1/5)
Are slopes 3/2 and 2/3 perpendicular? (expected answer: no; they multiply to 1, not −1)
notes.watch: Students often do only half the job: they flip 2 to 1/2 or change it to −2. Have them check that the product is −1 every time.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Through a Point
slides.board:
Line L: y = 4x − 1. Write the equation of the line through (2, 3) that is

(a) parallel to L    (b) perpendicular to L
steps: (a) Parallel: same slope, 4. Put the point into y = 4x + b: 3 = 4(2) + b, so 3 = 8 + b and b = −5.
(b) Perpendicular: the opposite reciprocal of 4 is −1/4. 3 = (−1/4)(2) + b, so 3 = −1/2 + b and b = 3 1/2 = 7/2.

notes.say: The question gives you a line, but it is only there to hand you a slope. Step one: decide the new slope, the same for parallel, or the opposite reciprocal for perpendicular. Step two: use the given point to find b. Notice that b does not have to be a whole number; 7/2 is fine.
ask: What is the new slope in part (b)? (expected answer: −1/4)
In part (a), why can't the answer be y = 4x − 1? (expected answer: that is line L itself; it does not pass through (2, 3))
notes.watch: A student who answers y = −4x + 11 for part (b) changed the sign but did not flip. Ask: “What do 4 and −4 multiply to?”

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Perpendicular Lines
slides.board:
Which equation represents the line that passes through (−3, 4) and is perpendicular to the line y = 3x − 2?

A. y = 3x + 13
B. y = (1/3)x + 5
C. y = −(1/3)x + 5
D. y = −(1/3)x + 3
steps: Eliminate A: its slope is 3, the same as the given line. It passes through (−3, 4), but it is parallel, not perpendicular.
Eliminate B: the slope 1/3 is flipped but the sign was not changed. 3 × 1/3 = 1, not −1.
Eliminate C: the slope is right, but b is wrong. (−1/3)(−3) is +1, not −1. Test the point: −(1/3)(−3) + 5 = 1 + 5 = 6, not 4.
D is correct: slope −1/3 (3 × (−1/3) = −1). 4 = (−1/3)(−3) + b gives 4 = 1 + b, so b = 3. Check: 1 + 3 = 4.

notes.say: Here is a typical GED line question. Every wrong choice is built from a real mistake: using the parallel slope, doing half of the opposite reciprocal, or slipping on a sign. Work it out first, then check your choice by substituting the point. Substituting the point is the fastest check you have on the test.
ask: Which choice did you pick, and how did you check it? (expected answer: D; substitute x = −3 and get y = 4)
notes.answer: D. Perpendicular slope −1/3; 4 = (−1/3)(−3) + b = 1 + b, so b = 3: y = −(1/3)x + 3.
notes.watch: If the student picks C, have them substitute (−3, 4) into it; seeing 6 instead of 4 makes the sign slip obvious.

slides.title: Functions and Function Notation
slides.board:
• A function gives exactly one output for each input.
  • In a list or table: if an x-value repeats with a different y-value, it is not a function. Repeated y-values are fine.
  • Vertical line test: if any vertical line hits the graph more than once, it is not a function.
  • f(x) is read “f of x,” the output when the input is x. It is not f times x.
  • f(3) = 10 means the point (3, 10) is on the graph.

notes.say: A function is a machine: you feed it an input and it gives back one output, every time. If one input could give two different outputs, the machine is broken, and that relation is not a function. On a graph, slide a vertical line across: the curve y = x<sup>2</sup> − 3 shown here gets hit only once by the line x = 2, at (2, 1), and that is true everywhere, so it is a function. Function notation is just a label: f(2) asks “what comes out when 2 goes in?”
ask: Is {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 7)} a function? (expected answer: yes; each input appears once, and repeated outputs are fine)
Is a vertical line a function? (expected answer: no; one input has infinitely many outputs)
notes.watch: Students often think a repeated y-value breaks the rule. Correct it with a real example: two people can have the same birthday (same output), but one person cannot have two birthdays (one input, two outputs).

slides.title: Using Function Notation
slides.board:
g(x) = 5 − 2x and h(x) = 2x2 − 1

  1. Find g(4).
  2. Find x when g(x) = 11.
  3. Find h(−3).
steps: 1. Replace x with 4: g(4) = 5 − 2(4) = 5 − 8 = −3. The point (4, −3) is on the graph.
2. Set the output equal to 11: 5 − 2x = 11. Subtract 5: −2x = 6. Divide by −2: x = −3.

notes.say: Two kinds of questions use function notation. One gives you the input and asks for the output: replace x with the number, using parentheses, and compute. The other gives you the output and asks for the input: set the expression equal to that output and solve, just like last week. Pay attention to which one you are being asked.
ask: What does g(4) = −3 tell you about the graph? (expected answer: the point (4, −3) is on it)
In number 3, what is (−3)<sup>2</sup>? (expected answer: 9, not −9)
notes.watch: On number 3, the answer −19 comes from squaring −3 as −9. Insist on parentheses around a negative input.

slides.title: Function or Not? Together
slides.board:
Decide whether each relation is a function. Then answer number 4.

  1. {(3, 1), (4, 1), (3, 2)}
  2. {(−2, 5), (0, 5), (2, 5)}
  3. The vertical line x = −1
  4. f(x) = x2 + 4x. Find f(−1).
steps: 1. Not a function. The input 3 has two outputs, 1 and 2.
2. Function. Each input appears once. The repeated output 5 is allowed.
3. Not a function. The input −1 is paired with every y-value; it fails the vertical line test.

notes.say: Let's sort these together. For each relation, hunt for an input that shows up twice with different outputs. If you find one, it is not a function. Then we will finish with a quick evaluation.
ask: In number 2, does the repeated 5 break the rule? (expected answer: no; repeated outputs are fine)
In number 4, what is 4(−1)? (expected answer: −4)
notes.answer: (1) not a function   (2) function   (3) not a function   (4) −3
notes.watch: If the student says number 2 is not a function, return to the birthday example from slide 19.

slides.title: Reading Real-World Graphs
slides.board:
• Read the title and both axis labels (with units) first.
  • Rising = increasing   flat = no change   falling = decreasing
  • Steeper = faster change.
  • To compare two functions, find each one's rate of change (slope) and starting value (y-intercept).

notes.say: Read the graph like a story. This phone starts at 100 percent and falls 15 points an hour while it is in use. From hour 2 to hour 3 the line is flat, so the battery did not change: the phone was off. From hour 3 to 4 the line rises, so it was charging, 20 points in one hour. Then it falls again at 15 points an hour. Every piece has a slope, and the slope is the rate.
ask: During which hour did the battery change fastest? (expected answer: hour 3 to 4, a change of 20 points)
What is the rate of change from hour 0 to hour 2? (expected answer: −15 percentage points per hour)
notes.watch: Students sometimes read the highest point as the fastest change. Steepness, not height, shows speed.

slides.title: Comparing Two Functions
slides.board:
Plan A: C = 15m + 60 dollars for m months. Plan B is shown in the table. When do the plans cost the same?

Months (m)123
Plan B cost ($)255075
steps: Plan B rate: (50 − 25) / (2 − 1) = 25 dollars per month. Starting value: 25 − 25 = 0. Plan B is C = 25m.
Compare: Plan A has the smaller rate (15 < 25) but the larger starting value (60 > 0).
Check: Plan A: 15(6) + 60 = 150. Plan B: 25(6) = 150. Both cost $150 at 6 months. Before 6 months Plan B is cheaper; after 6 months Plan A is cheaper.

notes.say: The GED loves to give one function as an equation and another as a table or a graph. Turn each one into the same two numbers: rate and starting value. Then the comparison is easy. The point where the two graphs cross is where the costs are equal, and that is the same as solving the system from last week.
ask: Which plan is cheaper for a 10-month contract? (expected answer: Plan A: 15(10) + 60 = $210 vs. Plan B: $250)
notes.watch: Students often say Plan B is always cheaper because it starts at $0. The graph shows the lines crossing; a smaller starting value does not mean cheaper forever.

slides.title: Your Turn: Equations of Lines
slides.board:
Four minutes. Write equations in y = mx + b form.

  1. Find the slope and y-intercept of 4x + 2y = 10.
  2. Slope 3, through (1, −2)
  3. Parallel to y = −x + 4, through (2, 6)
  4. Perpendicular to y = 3x + 2, through (3, 0)

notes.say: Your turn. You have four minutes. For each one, decide the slope first, then use the point to find b. Check each answer by putting the point back into your equation.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: slope −2 and (0, 5); y = 3x − 5; y = −x + 8; y = −(1/3)x + 1)
notes.answer: (1) 2y = −4x + 10, so y = −2x + 5: slope −2, y-intercept (0, 5)   (2) −2 = 3(1) + b, so b = −5: y = 3x − 5   (3) slope −1: 6 = −2 + b, so b = 8: y = −x + 8   (4) slope −1/3: 0 = (−1/3)(3) + b = −1 + b, so b = 1: y = −(1/3)x + 1
notes.watch: On number 1, y = −4x + 5 means only the constant was divided by 2. On number 4, y = (1/3)x − 1 means the sign was not changed.

slides.title: Your Turn: Functions and Graphs
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. f(x) = 7 − 3x. Find f(−2).
  2. Is {(−1, 4), (0, 4), (1, 4), (−1, 2)} a function?
  3. Function A is y = 6x + 1. Function B is linear and passes through (0, 2) and (2, 16). Which has the greater rate of change?

notes.say: Last practice round before the GED question. Three minutes. On number 3, you need the rate of change of each function, so find the slope of B from its two points.
ask: Read me your answers and your reason for number 2. (expected answer: 13; no, because −1 has two outputs; Function B)
notes.answer: (1) f(−2) = 7 − 3(−2) = 7 + 6 = 13   (2) No. The input −1 has two outputs, 4 and 2.   (3) B's rate is (16 − 2) / (2 − 0) = 14/2 = 7, and 7 > 6, so Function B.
notes.watch: On number 1, the answer 1 comes from 7 − 6: the student read −3(−2) as −6. On number 3, a student who says A has the greater rate may have compared the 14 (change in y) to 6 without dividing, or picked A because 6 > 2 compares a slope with an intercept.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Comparing Functions
slides.board:
The graph shows the cost of renting a pressure washer from Company P. Company Q charges $12 plus $8 per hour. Which statement is true?

A. Company P charges a greater hourly rate than Company Q.
B. Company Q is cheaper than Company P for rentals longer than 4 hours.
C. Company P and Company Q charge the same amount for a 4-hour rental.
D. Company Q costs $8 more than Company P for every hour of rental.
steps: First, Company P from the graph: rate (26 − 20) / 1 = $6 per hour; starting value $20. P: C = 6h + 20. Q: C = 8h + 12.
Eliminate A: P's rate is $6 and Q's is $8. The $20 is P's starting fee, not its rate.
Eliminate D: $8 is Q's whole hourly rate. Q's rate is only $8 − $6 = $2 more per hour than P's.
Eliminate B: it is backward. After the lines cross, the company with the greater rate (Q) costs more. At 5 hours: P = $50, Q = $52.
C is correct: 6h + 20 = 8h + 12 gives 8 = 2h, so h = 4. P: 6(4) + 20 = $44. Q: 8(4) + 12 = $44.

notes.say: This is a comparing-functions question with one function as a graph and one in words. Turn both into rate and starting value, and then every statement can be tested with numbers. Do not choose a statement because it sounds reasonable; check it.
ask: What is Company P's rate, and how did you find it? (expected answer: $6 per hour; the cost goes up $6 each hour on the graph)
Which choice is correct? (expected answer: C)
notes.answer: C. P: C = 6h + 20; Q: C = 8h + 12. Equal when 2h = 8, h = 4, at $44 each.
notes.watch: Choice A traps students who read the y-intercept as the rate. Choice B traps students who know the lines cross at 4 but guess which side is cheaper; have them test h = 5.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Use the Formula Sheet and Test a Point
slides.board:
1. Formula sheet: it lists the slope formula, slope-intercept form, and point-slope form. Use it.
  2. Sketch a quick graph: does the line rise (positive slope) or fall (negative)?
  3. Test a point: substitute a known point into each answer choice. If it does not work, cross the choice out.
  4. Calculator: on the TI-30XS, put a negative input in parentheses: (−3)2 = 9.

notes.say: Three habits will save you points on every graphing question. First, the formulas are given to you; open the formula sheet instead of trusting memory under pressure. Second, a ten-second sketch tells you the sign of the slope, which eliminates half the choices. Third, when the question asks which equation fits, substitute a point you know into each choice; it catches the sign slips that make every wrong answer look right. On the calculator, use the negative key and parentheses for negative inputs, or the calculator will square the 3 and then make it negative.
ask: Which equation passes through (2, 1): y = 3x − 5 or y = 3x + 1? (expected answer: y = 3x − 5, because 3(2) − 5 = 1)
notes.watch: Some students skip the point test because it feels slow. Time it once: it takes about five seconds per choice and catches most sign errors.
